USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 dinner with Xi to open a time-limited negotiating track without new unilateral commitments. Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and do not pre-commit to cancelling the scheduled January 1 List 3 step-up or to a purchase-only deal; make any pause of the 10-to-25 percent hike contingent on a written work program with dates and enforcement, not another May-style handshake. Do not launch the threatened additional ~$267 billion list before talks are tested.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly above neutral, not high. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B after List 3 took effect at 10% on 2018-09-24, with a legal step-up to 25% set for 2019-01-01 and a further ~$267B list still unused, so Washington still holds unused tariff leverage (timeline 2018-09-17/24; USTR/Federal Register). The core US real economy is not in a tariff recession: industrial production is ~104.1, Michigan sentiment is still 97.5, and CPI is contained. What is biting US interests is concentrated and political: China’s matching retaliation on soy/autos/aircraft has collapsed soybean sales to China by ~94% (China normally takes ~60% of US soy, ~$12B), with harvests rotting or being plowed under and only a fraction of the $12B farm-aid package paid by mid-November. Markets are also signaling cost: VIX is ~18.5 (up ~45% in the window), Baa yields have risen to 5.28%, WTI has fallen to ~$50, and the dollar is stronger. That is farm-belt and financial-volatility pain, not existential supply-chain or ally-cohesion failure — hence +0.12, not +0.5.

Action should be negotiate, not escalate or concede. Escalating into the G20 (or locking in the January hike before Xi is tested) would likely draw further farm/consumer retaliation and a full-coverage tariff war just as APEC already failed to produce a communiqué and China’s Q3 growth has slowed to 6.5% with the yuan ~9% weaker — i.e., Beijing is under pressure and may bargain, but a purchase-only truce already collapsed on 2018-05-29 after the 2018-05-19 joint statement. China’s 142-point list is judged by US officials as lacking timetable and enforcement. Therefore hold the current tariff stock, refuse unilateral rollback or purchase concessions, and use Buenos Aires to explore a delay of the January step-up only against verifiable structural talks.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 dinner with Trump to seek a time-limited truce that delays the 1 January 2019 jump of List 3 from 10% to 25%, and keep staff talks open. Do not add new tariffs or non-tariff measures now, and do not table a larger unilateral purchase or structural package until Washington puts a matching tariff pause on the table. Hold the existing retaliatory schedule as leverage, and treat any additional items beyond the 142-point list as bargaining chips rather than pre-summit gifts.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined US Section 301 coverage is already about $250B of Chinese exports after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 September, with that rate scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 January 2019 and a further ~$267B tranche threatened if talks fail (timeline 2018-09-17/24; CNN 27 Nov; NYT 27 Nov). That maps to the CHN +0.5 anchor: major export sectors are hit and a national champion (ZTE) was briefly denied US components in April, even though the ZTE denial order was later lifted after a large fine. Official Q3 GDP slowed to 6.5%, the weakest since 2009, and October data showed autos -11.7% y/y, property floor space sold -3.1%, and a further durables/electronics slump (CNBC 19 Oct; SCMP 23 Nov). The yuan has been allowed to weaken toward the psychologically important 7 per dollar level, forcing PBOC defense tools (counter-cyclical factor, short-yuan reserve requirements) rather than a clean export offset (SCMP 30 Oct). Reserves have not collapsed and the 2018 growth target is still in reach, so this is not a financial-stability or legitimacy crisis — hence 0.48 rather than 0.7+. Action should stay near zero because further retaliation would give Washington an easier pretext to execute the $267B threat and the January rate hike, while a large pre-emptive concession is premature: Trump already called the 142-item list “not acceptable” and said four or five large items remain (NYT 16 Nov), and the May 19 “trade war on hold” statement collapsed ten days later when the White House proceeded with 301 tariffs (timeline 2018-05-19/29). The 1 November phone call already locked in a leaders’ meeting; the disciplined move is to negotiate for a pause without new commitments.
